s0101: Intelligent and wise with great magnanimity; he was esteemed by his uncles and elder brothers.
Clever, far-sighted, and magnanimous, he was held in honor by his uncles and elder brothers.
s0102: His government honored leniency and simplicity; the common people embraced and submitted to him.
He governed with leniency and ease, and the people gave him their hearts.
s0103: He ruled the state one year and died.
He reigned one year and died.
s0104: Emperor Zhao, taboo name Luoguan, took the throne—son of the Founding Ancestor.
Emperor Zhao, styled Luoguan, was enthroned—son of the Founding Ancestor.
s0105: He divided the state into three parts: the emperor himself kept one part in the east, north of Shanggu, west of the Ru source, bordering the Yuwen tribe to the east;
He split the realm into three domains: the emperor kept the eastern third himself, north of Shanggu and west of the Ru River, with the Yuwen tribe on his eastern flank;
s0106: he assigned the eldest son of Emperor Wen, Emperor Huan, taboo name Yiyi, to lead one part, dwelling north of Canhepo in Dai commandery;
he gave Emperor Wen's eldest son, Emperor Huan, styled Yiyi, one third, with his seat north of Canhe Marsh in Dai commandery;
s0107: he assigned Emperor Huan's younger brother Emperor Mu, taboo name Yilu, to lead one part, dwelling at the old city of Shengle in Dingxiang.
and he gave Emperor Huan's younger brother, Emperor Mu, styled Yilu, the third, based at the old capital of Shengle in Dingxiang.
s0108: From the Founding Ancestor onward they had been at peace with Jin; the people were secure, wealth and livestock abundant, with more than four hundred thousand mounted archers.
Since the Founding Ancestor's day they had lived at peace with Jin; the people prospered, herds and stores were full, and they could field more than four hundred thousand horse archers.
s0109: That year Emperor Mu first left Bing province, moving various Hu peoples north to Yunzhong, Wuyuan, and Shuofang.
That year Emperor Mu marched out of Bing province and resettled mixed non-Han peoples north into Yunzhong, Wuyuan, and Shuofang.
s0110: He also crossed the river westward to attack the Xiongnu, Wuhuan, and other tribes.
He also crossed the Yellow River west to strike the Xiongnu, Wuhuan, and other tribes.
s0111: From eighty li north of Xingcheng to the Great Wall plain, boundary stones were set along the road to mark the border with Jin.
From eighty li north of Xingcheng to the edge of the Great Wall, they set up boundary markers along the road to divide their land from Jin.
s0112: In the second year they buried Emperor Wen and Empress Lady Feng.
In the second year they interred Emperor Wen and Empress Feng.
s0113: Earlier Emperor Si had wished to rebury them, but before accomplishing it he died.
Earlier Emperor Si had planned a reburial, but died before it could be done.
s0114: Now they fulfilled his earlier intention.
At last they carried out what he had intended.
s0115: Sima Ying the Prince of Chengdu sent Attendant-in-Ordinary Tian Si; Sima Yong the Prince of Hejian sent Commandant Jin Li; Sima Teng the Inspector of Bingzhou sent Registrar Liang Tian—all came for the funeral.

Sima Ying, Prince of Chengdu, sent Tian Si as attendant-in-ordinary; Sima Yong, Prince of Hejian, sent Commandant Jin Li; Sima Teng, inspector of Bingzhou, sent registrar Liang Tian—all to attend the burial.
s0116: From near and far two hundred thousand came to attend.
Nearly two hundred thousand mourners came from near and far.
s0117: In the third year [2] Emperor Huan crossed the desert on a northern tour and thereupon campaigned west against the various states.
In the third year [2] Emperor Huan crossed the northern desert on campaign and turned west to subdue the western states.
s0118: In the fourth year Beinarou the great chief of the eastern Weinü entered and settled in Liaodong.
In the fourth year Beinarou, great chief of the eastern Weinü, moved into Liaodong.
s0119: In the fifth year Xunniyan, son of Yuwen Mohuang, came to pay tribute.
In the fifth year Xunniyan, son of Yuwen Mohuang, presented tribute.
s0120: The emperor commended his sincerity and gave his eldest daughter in marriage to him.
The emperor praised his good faith and gave him his eldest daughter in marriage.
s0121: In the seventh year Emperor Huan returned from the western campaign; more than twenty states had submitted—in all five years, and now he came back east.
In the seventh year Emperor Huan returned from the west; more than twenty states had submitted to him. Five years had passed, and at last he turned homeward.
s0122: In the tenth year Emperor Hui of Jin was compelled by Sima Ying the Prince of Chengdu to remain at Ye.
In the tenth year Emperor Hui of Jin was held at Ye by Sima Ying, Prince of Chengdu.
s0123: Liu Yuan, a separate branch of the Xiongnu, rebelled at Lishi and styled himself King of Han.
Liu Yuan, of a Xiongnu splinter line, rose at Lishi and proclaimed himself King of Han.
s0124: Sima Teng, Inspector of Bingzhou, came to beg troops; Emperor Huan led more than a hundred thousand horse, and the emperor also launched a great campaign at the same time to assist, thoroughly defeating Liu Yuan's host at Xihe and Shangdang.

Sima Teng, inspector of Bingzhou, begged for aid. Emperor Huan led more than a hundred thousand cavalry, and Emperor Zhao mobilized on the same scale; together they shattered Liu Yuan's forces at Xihe and Shangdang.
s0125: When Emperor Hui returned to Luoyang, Teng then dismissed the army.
When Emperor Hui was restored to Luoyang, Teng released the allied troops.
s0126: Emperor Huan made alliance with Teng east of the Fen and returned.
Emperor Huan swore alliance with Teng east of the Fen River and marched home.
s0127: He sent his aides Wei Xiong and Duan Fan west of Canhepo to pile stones into a pavilion and set up a stele to record the journey.
He had his ministers Wei Xiong and Duan Fan raise a stone pavilion west of Canhe Marsh and erect a stele to commemorate the campaign.
s0128: In the eleventh year Liu Yuan attacked Sima Teng; Teng again begged troops.
In the eleventh year Liu Yuan attacked Sima Teng, who again begged for troops.
s0129: Emperor Huan with several thousand light horse came to the rescue, beheaded Liu Yuan's general Qimu Tun, and Yuan fled south to Puzi.
Emperor Huan rode to the rescue with a few thousand light cavalry, slew Liu Yuan's general Qimu Tun, and Yuan fled south to Puzi.
s0130: Jin enfeoffed Emperor Huan as Great Chanyu with a golden seal and purple cord.
Jin invested Emperor Huan as Great Chanyu, granting a golden seal and purple ribbon.
s0132: The emperor was outstandingly heroic and of towering stature; horses could not bear his weight.
He was a heroic, towering figure—ordinary horses could not carry him.
s0133: He commonly rode in a secure carriage drawn by great oxen; the ox horns could hold a dan of grain.
He usually traveled in a secure cart pulled by huge oxen whose horns could hold a full stone of grain.
s0134: The emperor was once poisoned by gu; where he vomited an elm tree grew.
Once, after he had been poisoned, an elm tree sprang up where he had vomited.
s0135: There were no elm trees on the soil of Canhepo, so people considered it strange, and it is recorded to this day.
Canhe Marsh had no elms in its soil, so people marveled at it—a wonder still told in chronicles.
s0136: The emperor ruled his part for eleven years in all.
In all he ruled his domain eleven years.
s0137: Later Wei Chao, Marquis of Dingxiang, set up a stele at Dagancheng to extol his merits.
Later Wei Chao, marquis of Dingxiang, raised a stele at Dagancheng praising his achievements.
s0138: His son Pugen succeeded to the throne.
s0139: In the twelfth year Li Xiong of the Ba people usurped an imperial title in Shu, styling his state Dacheng.
In the twelfth year Li Xiong of the Ba seized an imperial title in Shu and called his realm Dacheng.
s0140: In the thirteenth year Emperor Zhao died.
In the thirteenth year Emperor Zhao died.
s0141: Murong Hui the Great Chanyu of the Tuohe sent envoys with tribute.
Murong Hui, Great Chanyu of the Tuohe, sent envoys bearing tribute.
s0142: That year the Jie barbarian Shi Le and Ji Sang, director of Jin's horse pastures, rebelled.
That year the Jie chieftain Shi Le and Ji Sang, overseer of Jin's stud farms, rose in revolt.
s0143: Emperor Mu was naturally outstanding and brave beyond others; after Emperor Zhao died he took overall charge of the three parts and unified them.
Emperor Mu was born extraordinary, his courage and stratagem surpassing other men. After Emperor Zhao's death he gathered the three domains into one rule.
s0144: In the first year Liu Yuan usurped an imperial title, styling himself Great Han.
In the first year Liu Yuan took the imperial title and called his state Great Han.
s0145: In the third year Liu Kun the Inspector of Bingzhou sent envoys, offering his son Zun as hostage.
In the third year Liu Kun, inspector of Bingzhou, sent envoys and offered his son Zun as hostage.
s0146: The emperor commended his intent and richly rewarded and returned the gift.
The emperor approved his loyalty and sent back lavish gifts.
s0147: The great chief of the Bai tribe rebelled and entered Xihe; Tiefo Liu Hu raised hosts at Yanmen in response, attacking Kun's Xinxing and Yanmen commanderies.
The Bai chieftain rebelled into Xihe; Liu Hu of the Tiefo Xiongnu mustered troops at Yanmen to join him and struck Kun's Xinxing and Yanmen commanderies.
s0148: Kun came to beg troops; the emperor sent his nephew Emperor Pingwen at the head of twenty thousand horse to assist Kun in attacking; they thoroughly defeated the Bai tribe;
Kun begged for troops. The emperor sent his nephew, who would become Emperor Pingwen, with twenty thousand cavalry to aid him. They routed the Bai;
s0149: next they attacked Liu Hu and slaughtered his encampments.
then turned on Liu Hu and destroyed his camps.
s0150: Hu gathered the remainder and fled west across the river, hiding in Shuofang.
Hu gathered what was left, fled west across the river, and hid in Shuofang.
s0151: Emperor Huai of Jin advanced the emperor to Great Chanyu and enfeoffed him as Duke of Dai.
Emperor Huai of Jin promoted him to Great Chanyu and enfeoffed him as Duke of Dai.
s0152: Because the enfeoffment was far from the state and the people were not contiguous, he asked Kun for the lands north of Gouzhu Pass.
His fief lay too far from the heartland and did not adjoin his people, so he asked Kun for the territory north of Gouzhu Pass.
s0153: Kun, relying on this attachment, was greatly pleased; he moved the people of Mayi, Yin'an, Loufan, Fanzhi, and Guo five counties south of the pass, reestablished cities and towns, and ceded all the land entirely—east adjoining Dai commandery, west connecting Xihe and Shuofang, [3] several hundred li square.

Kun, glad to have such an ally, resettled the people of Mayi, Yin'an, Loufan, Fanzhi, and Guo—the five counties—south of the pass, rebuilt their towns, and yielded the whole region: east to Dai commandery, west to Xihe and Shuofang, [3] a domain hundreds of li across.
s0154: The emperor then moved one hundred thousand households to populate it.
The emperor then relocated a hundred thousand families to fill the new lands.
s0155: Liu Kun again sent envoys begging troops to save Luoyang; the emperor sent twenty thousand foot and horse to assist; Sima Yue the Grand Tutor and Prince of Donghai declined on grounds of famine in Luoyang, and the army returned.

Liu Kun again begged troops to relieve Luoyang. The emperor sent twenty thousand infantry and cavalry, but Sima Yue, grand tutor and Prince of Donghai, pleaded famine in the capital and the force turned back.
s0156: That year Liu Yuan died; his son Cong usurped the throne.
That year Liu Yuan died and his son Cong seized the throne.
s0157: In the fourth year Xing Yan, gate officer of Liu Kun, seized Xinxing in rebellion, [4] drawing in Liu Cong.
In the fourth year Xing Yan, Liu Kun's gate officer, rebelled and held Xinxing, [4] calling in Liu Cong.
s0158: The emperor sent troops to attack; Cong retreated and fled.
The emperor sent troops against him; Cong withdrew in flight.
s0159: In the fifth year Liu Kun sent envoys begging troops to attack Liu Cong and Shi Le.
In the fifth year Liu Kun sent envoys begging troops to strike Liu Cong and Shi Le.
s0160: Because Kun was loyal and righteous, the emperor took pity and granted it.
Out of regard for Kun's loyalty, the emperor pitied him and agreed.
s0161: When Cong sent his son Can to raid Jinyang, killing Kun's parents and seizing the city, Kun came to report the disaster; the emperor was greatly angered and sent his eldest son Liuxiu, Pugen son of Emperor Huan, and Wei Xiong, Fan Ban, Ji Dan and others as vanguard, while the emperor himself commanded a great host of two hundred thousand as rear guard.

When Cong's son Can stormed Jinyang, killed Kun's parents, and took the city, Kun came with the news. The emperor was furious. He sent his eldest son Liuxiu, Emperor Huan's son Pugen, and Wei Xiong, Fan Ban, Ji Dan, and others in the van, while he himself followed with two hundred thousand men.
s0162: Can was afraid, burned baggage, and broke through to flee.
Can panicked, burned his supply train, and broke out in flight.
s0163: They loosed horse in pursuit, beheading his generals Liu Ru, Liu Feng, Jian Ling, Zhang Ping, and Xing Yan; corpses lay for several hundred li.
Pursuing cavalry cut down his generals Liu Ru, Liu Feng, Jian Ling, Zhang Ping, and Xing Yan; the dead stretched for hundreds of li.
s0164: Kun came to pay respects in thanks; the emperor treated him with ceremony.
Kun came to give thanks; the emperor received him with full ceremony.
s0165: Kun strongly urged advance; the emperor said: "Had I not come earlier, causing your parents to be killed, I would truly be ashamed before you.
Kun pressed him to march on. The emperor said, "If I had not come late—if your parents had not died on my account—I would be ashamed indeed.
s0166: Now you have recovered your prefecture; yet I came from afar, and men and horses are weary—wait until the final campaign.
You have won back your province, but my men and horses are spent after the long march. Wait until we strike the final blow.
s0167: Can the enemy be exterminated entirely?"
Can every foe be wiped out at once?"
s0168: He gave Kun more than a thousand each of horses, cattle, and sheep, a hundred chariots of orders, [5] and left elite troops to garrison before returning.
He presented Kun with more than a thousand horses, cattle, and sheep apiece, a hundred wagons of provisions, [5] left picked troops to garrison the city, and withdrew.
s0170: That year Jia Pi, Inspector of Yongzhou, and Yan Ding, Defender of Jingzhao, because Emperor Huai had been seized by Liu Cong, together enthroned the Prince of Qin Ye, elder brother's son of Emperor Huai, as heir apparent at Chang'an under the title of Provisional Government.

That year Jia Pi, inspector of Yongzhou, and Yan Ding, defender of Jingzhao—because Emperor Huai was Liu Cong's prisoner—set up Emperor Huai's nephew, Prince Ye of Qin, as heir apparent at Chang'an under a provisional regime.
s0171: The emperor again instituted martial law and made a new appointment with Kun for a great campaign.
The emperor again mobilized for war and fixed a new date with Kun for a joint offensive.
s0172: He ordered Kun himself to erect the Jin provisional government and divide the forces; the emperor would send a hundred thousand horse south from Jian'gu Valley west of Xihe, Jin's army east from Puban Ford, meeting at Pingyang, living on Cong's grain, to welcome and restore the Jin emperor.

Kun was to proclaim the Jin provisional government and array his forces. The emperor would lead a hundred thousand cavalry south through Jian'gu west of Xihe; Jin's army would cross east from Puban. They would meet at Pingyang, feed on Cong's grain, and restore the Jin emperor.
s0173: The plan was not carried out.
s0174: In the sixth year they walled Shengle as the northern capital and repaired old Pingcheng as the southern capital.
In the sixth year they fortified Shengle as the northern capital and restored old Pingcheng as the southern capital.
s0175: The emperor ascended the western hills of Pingcheng to survey the terrain; then a hundred li farther south on the south bank of the Sui River at Huangguadui they built New Pingcheng—Jin people called it Little Pingcheng—and stationed his eldest son Liuxiu there to command the southern part.

From the western heights of Pingcheng he studied the land, then moved a hundred li south to Huangguadui on the south bank of the Sui River and built New Pingcheng—Chinese called it Little Pingcheng—placing his eldest son Liuxiu there to govern the south.
s0176: In the seventh year the emperor again made an appointment with Liu Kun to meet at Pingyang.
In the seventh year he again fixed a rendezvous with Liu Kun at Pingyang.
s0177: When Shi Le captured Wang Jun, within the state there were more than ten thousand households of mixed Xiongnu Hu, many of Le's kind; hearing Le had taken Youzhou, they plotted rebellion to respond to Le; discovered, they were executed; the plan to attack Cong was thereby halted.

When Shi Le took Wang Jun, more than ten thousand Xiongnu and other Hu households within the realm—many of them Le's kin—heard he had seized Youzhou and plotted revolt in his favor. The plot was uncovered and the ringleaders executed; the campaign against Cong was abandoned.
s0178: In the eighth year Emperor Min of Jin advanced the emperor to King of Dai, established officials, with revenue from Dai and Changshan commanderies.
In the eighth year Emperor Min of Jin raised him to King of Dai, gave him a full court, and granted the revenues of Dai and Changshan commanderies.
s0179: The emperor resented the disorder of Cong and Le and was determined to pacify them.
He burned with anger at Cong and Le and meant to crush them.
s0180: Earlier the national custom had been lenient and simple; the people did not yet know prohibitions.
Before this the nation's ways had been easy and plain; the people scarcely knew law.
s0181: Now bright punishments and severe laws—among the tribes many offended by disobeying orders.
Now he proclaimed stern statutes, and across the tribes many fell afoul of his commands.
s0182: All who were late were punished by slaughter of the entire tribe; some families went together to the place of execution; asked "where are you going" they answered "we are going to be executed."
Anyone late to muster saw his whole tribe put to death. Whole households walked together to the killing ground; when asked, "Where are you going?" they answered, "To be put to death."
s0183: His awesomeness subdued things—all of this kind.
Such was the awe in which he held men and things.
s0184: Emperor Pingwen, taboo name Yulü, took the throne—son of Emperor Si.
Emperor Pingwen, styled Yulü, was enthroned—son of Emperor Si.
s0185: Striking in bearing, powerfully built, with great martial prestige and stratagem.
He was imposing in stature, mighty in frame, and masterful in war and counsel.
s0186: In the first year the year was in dingchou.
s0187: In the second year Liu Hu held Shuofang and came to invade the western part; the emperor met him in attack and thoroughly defeated him; Hu fled alone on horseback.
In the second year Liu Hu, entrenched in Shuofang, invaded the west. The emperor met him and routed him; Hu escaped alone on horseback.
s0188: His younger cousin Lugu led his tribe to submit inward; the emperor gave his daughter in marriage to him.
His younger cousin Lugu brought his people in submission; the emperor gave him a daughter in marriage.
s0189: Westward he absorbed the old lands of Wusun; eastward he swallowed west of Wuji; those who could draw bow and mount horse approached a million.
He absorbed the old Wusun lands in the west and seized the country west of Wuji in the east; bowmen and horsemen neared a million.
s0190: Liu Cong died; his son Can usurped the throne and was killed by his general Jin Zhun; Liu Yuan's clansman Yao usurped the throne.
Liu Cong died. His son Can seized the throne but was slain by his general Jin Zhun; Liu Yuan's kinsman Yao then took power.
s0191: Hearing Emperor Min of Jin had been killed by Yao, he turned to his ministers and said: "Now the Central Plains have no lord—is Heaven perhaps endowing us?"
When he heard that Emperor Min of Jin had been killed by Yao, he said to his ministers, "The heartland is masterless. Does Heaven mean to bless us?"
s0192: Liu Yao sent envoys seeking peace; the emperor would not accept.
Liu Yao sent envoys suing for peace; the emperor refused.
s0193: That year Sima Rui usurped the great position in Jiangnan.
That year Sima Rui seized the imperial seat south of the Yangtze.
s0194: In the third year Shi Le styled himself King of Zhao, sent envoys begging peace, asking to become brothers.
In the third year Shi Le declared himself King of Zhao and sent envoys seeking peace, proposing brotherhood.
s0195: The emperor beheaded his envoys to break off relations.
The emperor had the envoys beheaded and broke off relations.
s0196: In the fourth year Zhang Mao who had privately appointed himself Governor of Liangzhou sent envoys with tribute.
In the fourth year Zhang Mao, who had taken the title of governor of Liangzhou on his own authority, sent tribute.
s0197: In the fifth year the usurper Jin Sima Rui sent the envoy Han Chang to add lofty rank and regalia; the emperor refused.
In the fifth year the Jin usurper Sima Rui sent Han Chang to offer elevated rank and robes of honor; the emperor rejected them.
s0198: He drilled troops and reviewed arms, with intent to pacify southern Xia.
He trained his armies and sharpened his weapons, intending to conquer the southern lands.
s0199: The empress after Emperor Huan, fearing the emperor had won the people's hearts and that it would harm her own son, killed the emperor; he died—several tens of great ladies perished.
Emperor Huan's widow, fearing that his hold on the people's loyalty would endanger her son, had the emperor murdered. Dozens of high-ranking women died with him.
s0200: At the beginning of Tianxing he was honored as Taizu.
When the Tianxing era began, he was posthumously titled Taizu.
